Directions: Read the passage. Then answer each question that follows.
Context: In this passage from The Kite Fighters, Young-sup and Kee-sup are brothers who live in Korea in `1473`. They have both made kites to fly. Flying kites is an important tradition.
Title: [from] The Kite Fighters
Author: by Linda Sue Park
Content: Young-sup loved the feeling of a kite on a line. He liked the moment of launching when he stood perfectly still, feeling the wind at his back and the kite's desire to be in the air. He experimented constantly, teasing the line this way and that, holding the reel different ways, even turning his whole body at varied angles, to coax the kite into following his commands.

The wind was always his partner, `text(one)` he must strive to understand with the kite's help. Sometimes it was like a kitten, pawing gently at the kite, nudging across the sky. At other times it was a big dog, friendly and eager but too rough in its play. It would bat and swipe and seem to shake the kite in its jaws.

On many occasions the wind died completely. At those moments Young-sup could feel the line slacken just before the kite began to fall. A lightning reaction, where his hands reeled in almost before his mind had finished the thought, would find a freshet¹ of wind in another patch of the sky. Other times he discovered that the only way to stop the kite's fall was to give it more line, not less.
The kite was like a part of him - the part that could fly.

With the failure of his homemade kite, Young-sup was forced to borrow his brother's tiger when he wanted to fly. Kee-sup was willing enough to share, for he had given up altogether trying to learn to launch a kite on his own. Either his lack of skill or the naughty tok-gabi² made his kite crash `text(every time)`. Young-sup now helped with `text(each launch)`, and Kee-sup repaid the favor by allowing him to have a turn with the tiger.

Despite plenty of opportunities to fly, Young-sup was not content. More than anything he wanted a good kite of his own. `text(One)` afternoon as they walked home from the hillside, he silenced his pride and spoke. The words did not come easily.

“Brother, I was - I was truly a failure at making a kite. You made yours so well. Would you make `text(one)` for me?” He hesitated, then went on. “It would be such fun to be able to fly together instead of taking turns. And the tiger is magnificent. It would be a great honor to fly `text(one)` just like it.”
Kee-sup walked on, looking down at the ground, and did not answer for a few moments.
Young-sup opened his mouth to protest. Kee-sup held up his hand for silence, then halted there in the road to speak.
“I won't make `text(one)` for you. But I'll help you make `text(one)` of your own.”
